It calls these displacement effects narrow in scope but important because knowledge-intensive services are a growing share of middle-class jobs there, says AI is not yet replacing large numbers of jobs in most developing countries, and flags pressure on call-center and back-office outsourcing. In the most optimistic scenario AI raises potential growth in the 2020s from 1.2% to 3.6% a year in advanced economies and from 4.1% to 4.9% in developing countries.
evidence.limits: The jobs shares score existing tasks, not realized job loss; the report says they might understate AI's potential to complement workers because new tasks are not counted, and that other studies using the median occupation as the cutoff report higher shares. The job-posting evidence comes from a few studies (China, India, ChatGPT's launch) and is described as early; the report itself says definitive evidence that AI is accelerating growth, generating more and better jobs, or improving services at scale is hard to find. Growth gains are scenario estimates, not observations. This entry read the Overview, not the nine chapters.

relations.note: Cites a study finding generative AI cut India's white-collar job postings, hardest for entry-level workers: the same pattern, from posting data.

title: Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence
summary: Stanford researchers analyze ADP payroll records for 3.5 to 5 million full-time US employees through June 2026. They find no evidence of economy-wide job displacement, but employment of 22-25-year-olds in the most AI-exposed occupations is 19% below where it would be had it kept pace with less-exposed peers, mainly through reduced hiring. They call the results descriptive, not causal.

change.note: Updates the 2025 version through June 2026: the young-worker gap in exposed jobs widened from 15% to 19%; still no economy-wide displacement.

lenses.public: In this payroll sample, fewer young people are being hired into jobs most exposed to AI, while people already in those jobs are not leaving at higher rates.
lenses.policy: Aggregate employment looks stable while one group falls behind: the authors say moderate aggregate changes can mask larger ones in subgroups, and publish monthly indicators to track them.
lenses.research: Descriptive, not causal: the young-worker gap shrinks with an education control, partly predates ChatGPT, and is far larger in this payroll sample than in national surveys.
lenses.ideas: The authors float that AI substitutes for codified, school-taught knowledge and complements experience; if so, how do people gain experience when entry-level roles shrink?

quotes.text: Overall, we do not find widespread job displacement in occupations most exposed to generative AI. However, employment has declined substantially for early-career workers in the occupations most exposed to AI, including but not limited to software development and customer support.
quotes.speaker: erik-brynjolfsson
quotes.context: Discussion section: the three authors sum up what the payroll data show overall and for early-career workers.

quotes.text: Employment of young workers in AI-exposed jobs now stands 19% below where it would be had it kept pace with that of their less-exposed peers; experienced workers show no comparable gap.
quotes.speaker: erik-brynjolfsson
quotes.context: Section 2.2, Fact 2: the paper's headline result for ages 22-25, as the three authors state it.

quotes.text: Separation rates fell for both groups and, among young workers, fell at least as much in the most exposed occupations as in the least exposed, the opposite of what displacement would imply. The divergence instead reflects hiring, with the gap in hiring rates between more- and less-exposed young workers opening after 2022.
quotes.speaker: erik-brynjolfsson
quotes.context: Section 2.4, Fact 4: the authors on whether the gap comes from hiring or from separations.

quotes.text: Declines are concentrated in occupations where AI usage primarily substitutes for human tasks; where usage primarily complements workers, employment is flat or rising, especially for experienced workers.
quotes.speaker: erik-brynjolfsson
quotes.context: Section 2.5, Fact 5: the authors on automating versus complementary uses of AI, measured with Anthropic Economic Index usage data.

quotes.text: These patterns attenuate when controlling for education, show some divergent trends predating generative AI, and are more pronounced in the ADP analysis sample than in national survey benchmarks, with some evidence of consistent patterns in government administrative data. We interpret these facts as early, descriptive indicators—canaries in the coal mine—rather than causal estimates
quotes.speaker: erik-brynjolfsson
quotes.context: End of the abstract: the authors on what weakens the pattern and how far the six facts can be read as causal.

notes: We read the paper's main text in full and the online appendix's prose; the appendix figures and tables were not checked. The paper is dated August 2026, with no day. Claude, made by Anthropic, wrote this entry, and one of the paper's six facts (automating versus complementary use of AI) rests on Anthropic's usage data; the entry is not otherwise about Anthropic.

evidence.design: Descriptive comparison of monthly payroll records from ADP: a balanced panel of firms with 3.5 to 5 million full-time employees a month, January 2021 to June 2026. Occupations are grouped into five bands of AI exposure (task ratings made with GPT-4, plus Anthropic Economic Index usage data in which Claude labels conversations as automating or augmenting work), and employment is tracked by age group from November 2022. Robustness checks and comparisons with national surveys (Current Population Survey, American Community Survey) follow.
evidence.finding: No sign of widespread job losses: average employment in the sample rose about 6% between November 2022 and June 2026 (about 4% in the most exposed fifth of occupations). But employment of 22-25-year-olds in the most AI-exposed occupations is 19% below where it would be had it kept pace with less-exposed peers (15% in the July 2025 data), with no comparable gap for experienced workers. In levels, it fell about 11% in the two most exposed fifths while rising about 10% in the three least exposed. The gap runs through reduced hiring, not more separations, and is concentrated where AI use automates tasks rather than complements workers; compensation trends differ little by age or exposure.
evidence.limits: The authors call these early, descriptive indicators, not causal estimates. The young-worker gap shrinks when occupational education is controlled for (the most-exposed estimate falls from -0.18 to -0.09), part of the divergence predates ChatGPT, and the gap is far larger in this sample than in the American Community Survey (-0.132 against -0.022 for 2022-24). The sample leans toward large firms and AI-exposed occupations, base pay leaves out bonuses and equity, firm-level AI adoption cannot be observed, and within-firm estimates for the most exposed fifth are sensitive to data-pipeline choices and not significant under the 2025 filters, and the codified-versus-tacit knowledge measure is scored by a language model and called suggestive. The data are proprietary, and ADP may review the paper to prevent disclosure of confidential information.
evidence.replication: The authors say Census administrative data (Tucker, 2026) show consistent raw patterns by age and industry exposure. A study using online profiles and job postings (Lambert and Schindler, 2026) finds remote work attenuates the AI link; following that specification on ADP data, the authors do not reproduce it and attribute the difference to the data.

relations.note: Payroll data show an entry-level hiring gap in AI-exposed jobs, as the segment says, but no economy-wide displacement and only small base-pay differences.

title: The Employment Effects of a Guaranteed Income: Experimental Evidence from Two U.S. States
summary: Six authors report a randomized trial in Texas and Illinois: 1,000 low-income adults aged 21 to 40 received $1,000 a month with no conditions for three years, and 2,000 controls received $50. Recipients had about $1,900 a year less income besides the payments and were 4.2 points less likely to be employed (pooled estimate), with no gain in job quality.

change.note: Revised August 2026: unconditional cash cut employment by 4.2 points (pooled estimate) and work by 1-2 hours a week, with no job-quality gain.

lenses.public: Low-income adults given $1,000 a month with no conditions worked somewhat less and spent more, but did not get better jobs. The study is not about AI.
lenses.policy: Bears on income-support ideas for AI job loss: unconditional cash cut work moderately and did not improve job quality, but it tested low-income adults, not displaced workers.
lenses.research: The 4.2-point employment fall pools unemployment-insurance records with survey answers (surveys alone: 2.3 points). Partner-hours results were not pre-specified and lose significance after the paper's multiple-testing correction.
lenses.ideas: The authors read the fall in work as recipients valuing time away from it, raising whether less paid work is a cost to offset or a choice to respect.

people.title: University of Michigan Ross School of Business and NBER

quotes.text: Overall, our results suggest a moderate labor supply effect that does not appear offset by other productive activities.
quotes.speaker: eva-vivalt
quotes.context: The authors' overall conclusion, in the abstract.

quotes.text: The transfer caused total individual income excluding the transfers to fall by about $1,900/year relative to the control group and a 4.2 percentage point decrease in labor market participation.
quotes.speaker: eva-vivalt
quotes.context: Abstract: the headline estimates for income and labor-market participation.

quotes.text: Despite asking detailed questions about amenities, we find no impact on quality of employment, and our confidence intervals can rule out even small improvements.
quotes.speaker: eva-vivalt
quotes.context: Abstract: on whether the cash let recipients find better jobs.

quotes.text: While decreased labor market participation is generally characterized negatively, policymakers should take into account the fact that recipients have demonstrated–by their own choices–that time away from work is something they prize highly.
quotes.speaker: eva-vivalt
quotes.context: Closing paragraph of the conclusion: the authors' advice to policymakers on reading the drop in work.

notes: Text saved by the research pass: NBER's landing page gave only the abstract, so the full working paper text was used. It is the August 2026 revision; NBER lists earlier versions (July 2024, January 2025, September 2025, January 2026), so figures can differ from earlier coverage. Read: sections I to VII and Tables III to V; the appendices (tables A.1 to A.68 and further figures) were not read in detail. The 4.2-point figure is the paper's pooled estimate and its preferred measure; the abstract calls it labor market participation, the body calls it employment. Partner hours appear plainly in the abstract, but the body says they were not pre-specified. Two of the six authors work at OpenResearch, whose name the study carries (the OpenResearch Unconditional Income Study); the program itself was implemented by two nonprofits. The paper names its funders only as the NSF and private donors. The body does not discuss AI (an appendix uses GPT only to recode free-text time-use answers), so any link to AI job loss is ours, not the authors'. The saved text keeps the PDF's line breaks and some hyphenation. The author id sarah-miller is the University of Michigan author; check it against other people of that name.

evidence.design: Randomized trial of a program implemented by two nonprofits in ten counties of north central Texas and nine of northern Illinois. 1,000 adults aged 21-40, with 2019 household income up to 300% of the federal poverty level, were randomly assigned to $1,000 a month with no conditions from November 2020 to October 2023; 2,000 controls received $50 a month. Outcomes come from state unemployment-insurance records (for participants who consented to linkage and could be matched), enumerated surveys (response rates 97% at midline, 96% at endline), online surveys and a phone-app time diary. Pre-registered.
evidence.finding: Relative to controls, total individual income excluding the transfers fell by about $1,900 a year (5.6% of the control mean). Employment fell 4.2 percentage points in the pooled records-and-survey estimate (2.3 points in surveys alone, 6.6 in records alone), and hours worked fell by 1-2 a week (1.3 in the survey measure). The extra time went mainly to leisure. The authors find no change in job quality and rule out wage gains above 58 cents an hour, and no significant effect on degree attainment. Spending rose by about $287 a month; well-being gains in year one faded by years two and three.
evidence.limits: Participants were low-income adults aged 21-40 in parts of two states, not workers displaced by technology, and the paper does not study AI. Payments lasted three years; the authors say follow-ups are needed on what persists after payments end, on children, and on effects if a program ran at scale. Unemployment-insurance records miss some contract and gig work, and the 4.2-point figure depends on pooling them with surveys. The partner and household hours results were not pre-specified and are not significant after the paper's multiple-testing correction. A working paper, not peer-reviewed.

title: Artificial intelligence in UK businesses: 2023 to 2026
summary: The Office for National Statistics analyses its Business Insights and Conditions Survey. Self-reported AI use among UK firms with 10 or more employees rose from around 12% (September 2023) to around 35% (June 2026); of firms using AI to improve operations, 63% report no change in headcount, 1% more and 6% fewer.

change.note: Among UK firms with 10+ employees, self-reported AI use reached about 35% by June 2026; 6% of those using it for operations report fewer staff.

lenses.public: About a third of UK firms with 10 or more employees say they use AI; among those using it to improve operations, 6% report fewer staff and 63% no change.
lenses.policy: The national statistics office calls AI measurement a work in progress and aims to identify its priority measurement topics by March 2027.
lenses.research: The headline figure counts any reported AI technology equally and the survey excludes finance, public services and other sectors, so it shows neither depth of use nor the whole economy.

quotes.text: The self-reported use of artificial intelligence (AI) in UK businesses with 10 or more employees has increased from around 12% to around 35% since late 2023, with larger firms more likely to have adopted AI.
quotes.speaker: office-for-national-statistics
quotes.context: First of the article's main points, on self-reported AI use between September 2023 and June 2026.

quotes.text: Of businesses using AI to improve business operations, 63% reported no change in worker headcount, while 1% reported increased headcount and 6% reported decreased headcount. These early indications show that the impact on employment remains limited at this stage.
quotes.speaker: office-for-national-statistics
quotes.context: From the section on labour market effects; chart figures are from the June 2026 survey wave.

quotes.text: Around 10% of businesses report automating or replacing roles with AI technologies, with relatively little variation across size bands.
quotes.speaker: office-for-national-statistics
quotes.context: From the section on integrating AI skills; the text does not say whether the share is of all businesses or only those using AI.

quotes.text: While this offers a consistent baseline, it treats all reported uses as equivalent and does not distinguish between light use, user-level use, and more embedded, production-level adoption.
quotes.speaker: office-for-national-statistics
quotes.context: From the data quality section: how the survey measures AI use, which affects how its headline adoption figure can be read.

quotes.text: However, some industries are excluded from BICS, such as agriculture, oil and gas extraction, energy generation and supply, public administration and defence, public provision of education and health, and finance and insurance.
quotes.speaker: office-for-national-statistics
quotes.context: From the data quality section: sectors the survey does not cover.

notes: Full article read from the page; the charts are images, so figures come from the text only. The headcount shares for firms using AI to improve operations (63%, 1%, 6%) add to 70%; the text does not say what the rest answered, so check the chart data. The base of the "around 10%" figure for automating or replacing roles is not stated in the text. The page gives the survey wave as 5 to 28 June 2026 in the chart source lines but 15 to 28 June in the chart titles, so only June 2026 is stated here. No individual author is named (Macroeconomic Insights team), so the organization is the speaker. Found no earlier Base entry that this clearly bears on.

evidence.design: Analysis of the ONS Business Insights and Conditions Survey (BICS), a voluntary fortnightly survey of UK businesses; the June 2026 wave (Wave 159) had a 26.7% response rate, with 38,637 businesses responding. Headline AI use is whether a business reports using any of a list of AI technologies; most figures cover businesses with 10 or more employees. Business answers are set beside an ONS survey of employees (Opinions and Lifestyle Survey, May to June 2026).
evidence.finding: Self-reported AI use among businesses with 10 or more employees rose from around 12% (September 2023) to around 35% (June 2026); by size, 28% of businesses with 0 to 9 employees and 49% of those with 250 or more report AI use. Adopters use about 1.6 AI technologies on average, up from 1.4. Among businesses using AI to improve operations, 63% report no change in headcount, 1% an increase and 6% a decrease; around 10% of businesses report automating or replacing roles with AI. Only 10% of AI-using businesses report extensive use. 55% of employees report using AI for work or education, against 35% of businesses.
evidence.limits: Headcount answers are what firms report in a survey, and the article notes a notable share say the effect is uncertain or not applicable. It does not say whether the 10% automating or replacing roles is of all businesses or only AI users. The survey leaves out agriculture, energy, public administration and defence, public education and health, and finance and insurance. The AI measure treats all uses as equivalent and does not separate light from production-level use. The questions on extent of use are new and the authors call results early indications. The series is labelled official statistics in development.

title: OECD Employment Outlook 2026: Geographic Disparities in Jobs and Incomes
summary: In its Employment Outlook 2026, the OECD finds the unemployment gap between young college graduates and other workers has widened since before the pandemic in every country it studied, with no turn when firms began using large language models. It concludes that their role in young people’s difficulties appears limited so far.

change.note: Cross-country comparison of timing finds no turn in graduates’ unemployment gap when firms adopted language models; weighs against the AI explanation.

lenses.public: Across OECD countries employment is near record levels, yet young graduates face a growing unemployment risk that, the OECD says, began before generative AI spread.
lenses.policy: On this summary page, the policy advice centers on regional mobility, local skills and industry strategies, and non-compete clauses, not on AI-specific measures.
lenses.research: The summary says the graduate trend predates generative AI but gives no method or figures; the underlying chapter, which we have not read, is needed to weigh the claim.

quotes.text: So far, the role of recent advances in large language models (LLM) in explaining the difficulties facing young people appears to be limited.
quotes.speaker: oecd
quotes.context: The report’s key findings, on young people entering the labour market.

quotes.text: Data from Australia, Canada, the European Union and the United States suggest that the role of LLMs in explaining the unemployment gap of young labour market entrants remains limited, both for those with and without a graduate degree.
quotes.speaker: oecd
quotes.context: Chapter 1, section 1.3.1, which compares firms’ AI hiring with young entrants’ unemployment and with job postings.

quotes.text: it can be concluded that LLMs diffusion is unlikely to be the main factor behind the increase in the unemployment gap for college graduates.
quotes.speaker: oecd
quotes.context: Section 1.3.1, after noting no turning point in the gap around the dates firms began using LLMs intensively.

quotes.text: To date, evidence on this subject is mixed and focusses mainly on the United States.
quotes.speaker: oecd
quotes.context: Section 1.3.1, on the research about generative AI and early-career employment.

notes: The full report PDF (fetched directly; the HTML pages refuse scripts). We read the key findings and Chapter 1, section 1.3 (young labour market entrants), not the whole report. Quotations are the OECD’s own words, from the PDF text.

evidence.design: The OECD’s annual review of labour markets. Chapter 1, section 1.3, compares the timing of firms’ AI hiring (LinkedIn data, a proxy for AI use) with young entrants’ unemployment gaps and with job postings in occupations exposed to large language models, in Australia, Canada, the EU, New Zealand, the UK and the US.
evidence.finding: The unemployment gap between young college graduates and the working-age population has widened since before the pandemic in every country analysed, well before firms turned to LLMs, with no turning point around mid-2023 to early 2024 when firms’ use of LLMs rose sharply. The OECD concludes LLMs are unlikely to be the main factor.
evidence.limits: A comparison of trends and timing, not a causal estimate; AI hiring on LinkedIn is a proxy for firms’ AI use. The OECD notes the wider evidence is mixed and mostly from the United States.

title: Remote Work Leaves Younger Workers Sidelined
outlet: Liberty Street Economics (Federal Reserve Bank of New York)
summary: In a New York Fed blog post, Natalia Emanuel, Emma Harrington and Amanda Pallais argue that remote work, more than generative AI, explains the rise in unemployment among young college graduates. They estimate it accounts for 64% of the increase from 2017-19 to 2022-24, drawing on survey data and one company's records, and say AI may matter more later.

change.note: Offers remote work, not AI, as the main explanation: an estimated 64% of the rise in young graduates' unemployment, with timing cited as support.

lenses.public: For recent graduates, the post says rising unemployment owes more to remote work, which cuts training and mentoring, than to AI, though AI may matter more later.
lenses.policy: The post ties youth unemployment mainly to how firms organize work, such as return-to-office rules and mentoring, rather than to AI; its evidence on mechanism is from one large company.
lenses.research: Compares remotable with non-remotable occupations and holds AI exposure constant, but the 64% is a back-of-the-envelope figure and the mechanism evidence is from one firm.
lenses.ideas: The post treats a first job as training: when mentoring needs proximity, distance can shut young people out of the learning that later work depends on.

people.title: Research economist, Research and Statistics Group, Federal Reserve Bank of New York
Assistant professor of economics, University of Virginia

quotes.text: Since so many young college graduates are in remotable occupations, our back-of-the-envelope calculation indicates that remote work can explain 64 percent of the increase in unemployment for all young college graduates between 2017−19 and 2022−24.
quotes.speaker: natalia-emanuel
quotes.context: The post's estimate of how much of the rise in young graduates' unemployment remote work explains, with the authors' own label for the method.

quotes.text: Further, the timing of this surge suggests that remote work—not generative AI—explains the bulk of the rise in youth unemployment.
quotes.speaker: natalia-emanuel
quotes.context: Opening summary of the post, by its three authors: their reading of the timing of the rise in youth unemployment.

quotes.text: But the uptick in youth unemployment rates predates the rapid diffusion of AI. Moreover, even when we hold occupations’ exposure to AI constant, we find that the differences between younger and older workers persist in both remotable and non-remotable jobs.
quotes.speaker: natalia-emanuel
quotes.context: Section "The AI Factor": the authors on why generative AI is not the main explanation so far.

quotes.text: Of course, generative AI and other factors may play a more primary role in determining the employment patterns of younger workers going forward. Nonetheless, the evidence to date suggests that the rise of remote work has meaningfully contributed to the recent challenges facing young college graduates.
quotes.speaker: natalia-emanuel
quotes.context: Same section: the authors' caveat that AI may matter more later, and their conclusion on remote work.

quotes.text: Working with proprietary data from a Fortune 500 company, we are able to shed light on the underlying reasons for these labor market changes.
quotes.speaker: natalia-emanuel
quotes.context: Section "Patterns at the Firm Level": the authors on the single-company data behind their evidence on mentoring and hiring.

notes: We read the post and its disclaimer. Its two charts and their data were not checked, and reader comments on the page were not used.

evidence.design: Compares unemployment of college graduates under 29 with older graduates in US Current Population Survey data, splitting occupations by how easily their tasks can be done remotely and checking the result with occupations' AI exposure held constant. A back-of-the-envelope calculation gives the share explained by remote work. Evidence on how remote work affects feedback, mentoring, work quality and hiring comes from proprietary data from one Fortune 500 company, including its return-to-office mandates.
evidence.finding: Unemployment among graduates under 29 rose from 3.1% on average in 2017-19 to 3.7% in 2022-25, while it edged down for more experienced graduates (1.9% to 1.8%). The rise is concentrated in occupations that can be done remotely (almost 1 percentage point, 2017-19 to 2022-24); in non-remotable jobs the young-old gap returned to baseline after 2020. The authors estimate remote work explains 64% of the increase between 2017-19 and 2022-24. They say the rise predates the rapid spread of generative AI and that the age gap persists with AI exposure held constant. At the company studied, distance cut feedback and mentoring, and distributed teams hired more experienced workers even after offices reopened.
evidence.limits: The 64% is a back-of-the-envelope figure, and the evidence on mechanism comes from one Fortune 500 company. The authors say generative AI and other factors may play a more primary role going forward. Outside that company, the case rests on timing and comparisons across occupation groups. It is a blog post, and the page says its views are the authors' and not necessarily those of the New York Fed or the Federal Reserve System.

title: What We Do and Don't Know About How AI is Affecting the Labor Market
summary: The Budget Lab at Yale compares employment, wages and unemployment in AI-exposed occupations with a weighted group of unexposed occupations, using Current Population Survey data. Gimbel, Kendall and Nunn report no statistically or economically significant effect so far, and caution that exposure measures are imperfect, the survey is thin for narrow groups, and the picture could change quickly.

change.note: First Budget Lab estimates of AI's effect: no significant change in exposed occupations' employment or wages; a positive unemployment estimate is not statistically significant.

lenses.public: Jobs most open to AI show no significant change in employment or pay against a matched group of other jobs so far, though the authors say that could change quickly.
lenses.policy: This analysis gives lawmakers no clear AI effect on jobs or pay to cite yet; the Budget Lab says it will update as new labor market data arrive.
lenses.research: Exposure scores are informed guesses that can average away opposite effects, the design needs AI's arrival separable from events like remote work, and the survey is weak for narrow groups.

quotes.text: Using an approach called synthetic differences-in-differences (SDID) that addresses these challenges, we generally find no statistically or economically significant effects as of yet.
quotes.speaker: martha-gimbel
quotes.context: The authors' headline result, from the opening paragraphs: employment and wages in AI-exposed occupations compared with a weighted group of unexposed ones.

quotes.text: These figures indicate positive effects in the most recent quarter—roughly half a percentage point increase in the entire sample, and more for the 16-34 year old subsample—but both are statistically insignificant as of the first quarter of 2026.
quotes.speaker: martha-gimbel
quotes.context: From the main text, on the appendix figures for the unemployment rate in exposed occupations, for all workers and for ages 16 to 34.

quotes.text: This means that analysis of exposure metrics could actually hide effects if (for instance) half of “exposed” occupations see their jobs expand and half see their jobs contract—the average could be zero.
quotes.speaker: martha-gimbel
quotes.context: The authors explain why occupation-level exposure scores may miss real effects, which is why the Budget Lab's own tracker relies on other measures.

quotes.text: First, LLMs are constantly improving, such that the economic impacts from early models seem likely to be smaller than those of recent models.
quotes.speaker: martha-gimbel
quotes.context: The first of the caveats the authors list on their main finding.

quotes.text: If labor market effects of AI are currently limited to a narrow slice of the workforce, other datasets and research designs would be better suited to identify them.
quotes.speaker: martha-gimbel
quotes.context: The authors' closing caveat about what the Current Population Survey can detect in narrow groups such as recent graduates.

notes: Full article and appendix read from the page. The page names three authors and gives no individual roles; quotations are attributed to the first-named author on behalf of all three, and the title shown is the Budget Lab as the site gives it. The page says the Budget Lab will update the assessment, so check for a later version. The research pass's excerpt also mentions a Budget Lab tracker (updated 15 September 2026) and an October 2025 baseline report; neither is part of this page and neither is described here. Found no earlier Base entry that this clearly bears on.

evidence.design: Synthetic difference-in-differences on Current Population Survey data (2020 omitted). Occupations in the top third of the Budget Lab's AI-exposure ranking are compared, from ChatGPT's release in the fourth quarter of 2022 onward, with a weighted mix of occupations in the bottom third. Outcomes: employment share of the civilian population, median real hourly wages, and, in the appendix, unemployment rates, including ages 16-34.
evidence.finding: No statistically or economically significant effect of AI exposure on occupational employment or real hourly wages. For the latest quarter's employment share, the point estimate is virtually zero and the top of the 95% confidence interval is about 5% of the average exposed occupation's share (just above 0.16% of the civilian population). The estimated effect on unemployment in exposed occupations is positive in the latest quarter, roughly half a percentage point (more for ages 16-34), but not statistically significant as of the first quarter of 2026.
evidence.limits: Exposure scores are informed guesses and do not mark jobs at risk, so averaging could hide opposite effects within the exposed group. The method assumes AI's arrival can be told apart from other changes such as remote work, and the authors say impacts of early models seem likely to be smaller than those of recent ones. The Current Population Survey is underpowered for narrow groups: among 22-27-year-olds, few occupations met the 50-observations-per-quarter rule. Unemployment estimates by occupation are imprecise.

title: You’re (not) hired: Artificial intelligence and early career hiring in the Quarterly Workforce Indicators
summary: Lee C. Tucker's Census Bureau working paper compares industries by AI exposure in administrative employer-employee data. Hires of 22-24-year-olds in the most exposed fifth fell about 9% relative to others when ChatGPT was released and stayed down; their adjusted employment fell 12% over ten quarters. Tucker finds earlier trend shifts and advises some caution in attributing it all to AI.

change.note: Administrative data show hires of 22-24-year-olds in the most AI-exposed industries fell about 9% at ChatGPT's release and stayed down; causes are unsettled.

lenses.public: For young job-seekers, official records show fewer hires into AI-exposed industries since ChatGPT's release; the author cautions that remote work and schooling may also play a part.
lenses.policy: These data cannot separate AI from remote work or schooling; the author points to linking AI-adoption surveys with employer-employee records as the way to learn more.
lenses.research: Exposure is assigned by industry, not firm; hires fall at ChatGPT's release and interest-rate sensitivity explains little of that, yet triple-difference estimates show weakening from around COVID.
lenses.ideas: One mechanism the author floats: uncertainty about what AI can do may lead firms to hold back hiring of young workers, an effect that would precede widespread adoption.

quotes.text: Regression adjusted employment of early career workers in the most AI-exposed quintile of industry-state cells declined by 12% over the 10 quarters following the introduction of ChatGPT, even as employment in less exposed industries has remained stable.
quotes.speaker: lee-c-tucker
quotes.context: Abstract: the paper's main employment result for early-career workers in the most AI-exposed industry-state cells.

quotes.text: Using detailed tabulations from matched employer-employee administrative data, I document evidence of an immediate, sizable, and persistent decrease in the level of early career (22-24 year old) hires following introduction of ChatGPT within the industry-state cells that are most exposed to AI.
quotes.speaker: lee-c-tucker
quotes.context: Abstract: the paper's main hiring result, with the data it rests on.

quotes.text: However, triple difference estimates provide some evidence of earlier trend shifts on employment, hiring, and separations around the onset of the COVID pandemic. I discuss potential explanations, including the increase in remote work and increased educational attainment among workers in AI-exposed occupations.
quotes.speaker: lee-c-tucker
quotes.context: Abstract: the author on earlier trend shifts around the onset of COVID and on remote work and schooling as other explanations.

quotes.text: A historical decomposition suggests that up to one quarter of relative early career employment declines through 2025q2 may be attributable to monetary policy shocks through 2023, but the analysis does not find evidence that these shocks can explain the rapid decline in hires at the most AI-exposed firms in comparison to others.
quotes.speaker: lee-c-tucker
quotes.context: Abstract: the author on how much of the relative employment decline monetary policy could explain.

quotes.text: The results of this analysis encourage some caution in attributing all of this to AI.
quotes.speaker: lee-c-tucker
quotes.context: Conclusion, after noting that employers in the most exposed industries shed over 150,000 early career jobs in ten quarters.

notes: Dated April 2026 (CES Working Paper 26-27); the paper gives no day. The saved text comes from the PDF, which loses some letters in its body text, so quotations are taken from the abstract and from passages that extracted cleanly.

evidence.design: Event-study and triple-difference analysis of public Quarterly Workforce Indicators tabulations, which come from matched employer-employee administrative data covering a near-universe of private-sector jobs. Hires, separations, employment and earnings of 22-24-year-olds are compared across industry-by-state cells ranked into five bands of AI exposure (an occupation-level measure made with GPT-4 task ratings, converted to industries). A flows-based counterfactual and a local-projections test of sensitivity to monetary policy follow.
evidence.finding: Hires of 22-24-year-olds in the most AI-exposed fifth of industry-state cells fell about 9% right after ChatGPT's release, relative to less exposed cells, and had not recovered; over the last four quarters they were 12.7% below the reference level. Employment of 22-24-year-olds in that fifth fell 15.2% from 2022Q4 to 2025Q2 (12.4% regression-adjusted), about 159,000 jobs, which the paper says fewer hires fully account for. The hiring rate largely recovered by early 2025 only because the employment base had shrunk. Earnings growth of early-career workers in exposed industries slowed slightly. Employment of older workers in the same industries was comparatively unaffected.
evidence.limits: The author calls it premature to read the hiring drop as clear evidence of AI's long-run effect. Triple-difference estimates show young workers' hires, employment and separations were already weakening relative to older workers around the start of COVID, so remote work or delayed entry through schooling may play a role; a monetary-policy test suggests up to a quarter of the relative employment decline through 2025Q2 could reflect interest-rate shocks. Exposure is assigned by industry, not firm or worker, age bands are coarse, and firm-level AI adoption is not observed. Census states the paper has not had the review given to its publications.
evidence.replication: Section 3 replicates the Stanford payroll-data result in administrative data: the author calls the unadjusted 15.2% decline highly consistent with the 16% regression-adjusted estimate in that study's 2025 version.

relations.note: Administrative data also show an entry-level hiring drop in AI-exposed industries, but the author advises some caution in attributing all of it to AI.

title: The Microstructure of AI Diffusion: Evidence from Firms, Business Functions, and Worker Tasks
summary: Census Bureau and University of Maryland researchers analyze the 2026 AI supplement to the Business Trends and Outlook Survey. They report 18% of US firms using AI in a business function (32% employment-weighted); firms reporting task effects mostly describe augmentation, and about 2% of AI-using firms report AI-driven employment decreases. The authors call the regressions descriptive.

change.note: New Census survey data link firm adoption, business functions and worker tasks: 18% of firms use AI; AI-driven headcount cuts are reported by few.

lenses.public: Most US firms do not report using AI; among those that do, few say it has cut or added jobs, and task changes are mostly AI assisting staff.
lenses.policy: The survey's core AI questions were reworded in November 2025, so AI-use rates before and after cannot be compared directly, which limits trend claims about adoption.
lenses.research: Firm respondents report on workers, headcount effects carry no magnitudes, and regressions are descriptive; the authors say linking the survey to administrative microdata is the key next step.

people.title: University of Maryland and U.S. Census Bureau

quotes.text: During the supplement reference period (Nov 2025-Jan 2026), 18% of firms used AI in a business function, rising to 32% on an employment-weighted basis; adoption is expected to reach 22% within six months.
quotes.speaker: kathryn-bonney
quotes.context: From the abstract: firm-level adoption during the survey supplement's reference period.

quotes.text: AI-driven employment change instances remain modest, with only about 5% of AI-using firms reporting any headcount impact – distributed nearly equally between increases (2.3% firm-weighted and 3.7% employment-weighted) and decreases (2.0% firm-weighted and 2.4% employment-weighted).
quotes.speaker: kathryn-bonney
quotes.context: From the introduction's highlights: employment changes that firms using AI attribute to AI, over the last six months, as reported by firms.

quotes.text: Although AI correlates with superior firm performance, its current impact is defined primarily by task augmentation rather than substitution, leaving firm employment largely unaffected.
quotes.speaker: kathryn-bonney
quotes.context: The authors' overall assessment in the conclusion, based on firms' own reports of task and employment effects.

quotes.text: Functional breadth and operational investment are positively associated with employment decreases, whereas worker-task integration shows no significant link to headcount reduction once functional integration and operational investment are taken into account.
quotes.speaker: kathryn-bonney
quotes.context: From the abstract: regression results on employment; the paper says its regressions carry no causal interpretation.

quotes.text: An important limitation is that worker-use measures are reported by firm respondents rather than directly by employees and thus reflect firm-level assessments of worker behavior rather than independent worker reports.
quotes.speaker: kathryn-bonney
quotes.context: The authors' stated limitation of the survey, from the introduction.

notes: The PDF's text layer had dropped the fi, ff and fl ligatures in the body ("frms", "efects"); the saved text restores them by dictionary (about 900 words) and the quoted body passages were checked against page images of the PDF. The abstract and front matter were unaffected. Main text read in full; the appendices were skimmed. Quotations are attributed to the first author on behalf of all six. The abstract's "2% of firms" is, in the paper's text and Table 4, a share of AI-using firms. Haltiwanger was also a part-time Census Bureau employee when the paper was written, per its footnote. The research pass lists an NBER version (Working Paper 35141); that is not mentioned in the paper read. Found no earlier Base entry that this clearly bears on.

evidence.design: Analysis of the second AI supplement to the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey (BTOS), a nationally representative survey of US employer firms. Responses were collected from November 17, 2025 to February 8, 2026 (reference period November 2025 to January 2026), pooling a sample of more than 117,000 firms. AI use is measured at three layers: the firm, 15 business functions and worker tasks; the paper then summarizes task effects, builds indices, and runs regression-style summaries with fixed effects that it says carry no causal interpretation.
evidence.finding: 18% of firms used AI in a business function (32% employment-weighted) and 22% expected to within six months; in 23% of firms (41% employment-weighted) workers use AI in tasks. Use reaches 50%-60% among very large firms in Information, Professional Services and Finance. 57% of adopters use AI in three or fewer business functions. Of AI-using firms, 44% report augmenting tasks; among firms reporting any task effect, 66% only augment. About 5% of AI-using firms report any AI-driven headcount change: 2.0% decreases (2.4% employment-weighted) and 2.3% increases (3.7%), against 16% replacing software or equipment with AI. In regressions, functional breadth and operational investment are positively associated with employment decreases; worker-task breadth is not.
evidence.limits: Descriptive, not causal: the authors say regressions carry no causal interpretation. Worker use and headcount changes are reported by firm respondents, not employees, so decentralized use may be under-reported. Headcount answers give only the direction of change, with no magnitudes or gross worker flows. The core AI question was reworded in November 2025, so earlier waves are not directly comparable. Census states that its working papers have not had the review given to Census Bureau publications.

title: Anthropic Economic Index report: Learning curves
summary: Anthropic's Economic Index report, based on 1 million Claude.ai and 1 million first-party API conversations sampled on 5-12 February 2026, finds coding still the largest use of Claude, with personal use rising. It reports that longer-tenured users succeed more often and cautions that self-selection or survivorship may partly explain this.

change.note: New Claude usage measurements: coding still leads, use diversified, and longer-tenured users succeed more, though the authors flag self-selection and survivorship bias.

lenses.public: Anthropic's own counts show coding is the largest use of Claude and personal use is growing; longer-term users succeed more often, which could favor early adopters.
lenses.policy: One AI company's usage data, with a warning that unequal skill and access could widen inequality; it measures task use, not jobs lost or pay changes.
lenses.research: Comparisons within the same task find longer-tenure users succeed more, but success is Claude's own rating and the authors cannot separate learning from self-selection or survivorship.
lenses.ideas: The authors suggest benefits of early adoption may be self-reinforcing, raising a fairness question about who gets the chance to learn to use AI well.

people.title: Lead author, Anthropic Economic Index report
Lead author, Anthropic Economic Index report
Lead author, Anthropic Economic Index report

quotes.text: Coding remains the most common use on our platforms, with tasks associated with Computer and Mathematical occupations accounting for 35% of conversations on Claude.ai
quotes.speaker: anthropic
quotes.context: Anthropic's report on what Claude.ai is used for, from its February 2026 sample.

quotes.text: About 49% of jobs have seen at least a quarter of their tasks performed using Claude.
quotes.speaker: anthropic
quotes.context: Anthropic's report, summarizing how widely Claude is used across occupations; the same chapter says this barely changed since its previous sample.

quotes.text: Usage remains heavily concentrated: the top 20 countries account for 48% of all per-capita usage, up from 45%, underscoring a persistent gap in global adoption.
quotes.speaker: anthropic
quotes.context: Anthropic's report on how Claude use is spread across countries.

quotes.text: These results suggest that high-tenure users have more success in their Claude conversations, and that this is not due to simple factors like language or the task being performed.
quotes.speaker: anthropic
quotes.context: Anthropic's report on users who signed up at least six months earlier; the regressions put the gap at 3 to 5 percentage points.

quotes.text: Further, there’s an inherent survivorship bias: people who signed up a year before our data pull may be seeing positive results from their usage. We do not observe people who signed up a year ago but are no longer using Claude.
quotes.speaker: anthropic
quotes.context: Anthropic's report on a limit of its tenure comparison.

notes: Anthropic's own report about its own product, so the entry is marked as about Anthropic and written by Claude. The summary section says high-tenure users have a 10% higher success rate, while the regression section reports 3 to 5 percentage points; the text read does not reconcile the two (the appendix is a separate page and was not read), so check whether 10% is a relative figure. The page credits authors without individual titles and marks the first block as lead authors. The report refers to a separate labor-market-impacts report and to a previous Economic Index report from January 2026; neither was read here.

evidence.design: Company report from Anthropic's Economic Index. It classifies a sample of 1 million conversations from Claude.ai and 1 million from Anthropic's first-party API, collected on 5-12 February 2026, by the occupational tasks (O*NET) they involve, using a privacy-preserving analysis system, and compares them with earlier samples (November 2025 and August 2025). It also compares users who signed up at least six months earlier with newer users, with regressions that control for task, model, use case and country.
evidence.finding: Tasks tied to computer and mathematical occupations were 35% of Claude.ai conversations, and about 49% of jobs have seen at least a quarter of their tasks performed using Claude, barely changed since November 2025. The ten most common tasks fell from 24% to 19% of Claude.ai conversations; personal use rose from 35% to 42% and coursework fell from 19% to 12%. The average hourly wage of US workers who do the tasks seen on Claude.ai fell from $49.3 to $47.9. The top 20 countries account for 48% of per-capita usage, up from 45%. Users who signed up at least six months earlier had a success rate about 5 percentage points higher in a simple comparison, about 3 within the same task and about 4 with full controls (the report's summary calls this a 10% higher success rate). The authors say such differences in success could deepen inequalities in the labor market.
evidence.limits: Describes one company's users over one week in February 2026, which overlapped with a Super Bowl advertising push that brought many first-time users and, in some countries, a school winter break (which the authors say explains part of the fall in coursework). It counts which tasks Claude is asked to do and values them with US wage data; it does not observe employment or pay outcomes. Success is Claude's own assessment of whether a conversation succeeded. The authors say the experience-and-success pattern may reflect self-selection (early adopters may be more technical) or survivorship bias, since users who left are not observed, and that they cannot yet separate these from learning by doing.

title: Forecasting the Economic Effects of AI
summary: In a Chicago Fed working paper, researchers surveyed 69 economists, 52 AI industry and policy professionals, 38 superforecasters and 401 members of the public on AI's effects on the US economy. Unconditional forecasts stay near historical trends; under a rapid-progress scenario, economists forecast labor force participation falling to 55% by 2050. These are forecasts, not measurements.

change.note: Forecast survey of 69 economists, 52 AI experts, 38 superforecasters, 401 public: near-trend overall, widely uncertain if AI progress is rapid.

lenses.public: Surveyed economists and AI experts mostly expect modest change in jobs and growth, but widely uncertain outcomes if AI becomes far more capable; these are forecasts, not measurements.
lenses.policy: The authors note that policy cannot plan for the median: if AI progress is rapid, outcomes for growth and participation spread widely, including a possible deep fall in participation.
lenses.research: Scenario-conditional forecasts split disagreement about AI's pace from disagreement about its effects, finding the second larger; the authors judge scenario ambiguity a limited caveat.
lenses.ideas: Economists and the public want different remedies although they forecast broadly similar outcomes, so the choice between retraining, a job guarantee and basic income is not settled by forecasts alone.

quotes.text: The median respondent in each group expects substantial advances in AI capabilities by 2030, small declines in labor force participation consistent with demographic shifts, and an annual GDP growth rate of 2.5%, which exceeds both the typical medium-run (2.0%) and long-run (1.7%) baseline forecasts from government agencies and private-sector forecasters.
quotes.speaker: ezra-karger
quotes.context: Abstract: what the median respondent in each of the five surveyed groups forecasts before any AI-progress scenario is assumed. Survey respondents' forecasts, reported by the authors.

quotes.text: Conditional on a “rapid” AI progress scenario … experts forecast substantial, though not historically unprecedented, economic shifts: annualized GDP growth rising to around 4% and the labor force participation rate falling from its current level of 62% to 55% by 2050, with roughly half of that decline—equivalent to around 10 million lost jobs—attributable to AI.
quotes.speaker: ezra-karger
quotes.context: Abstract: forecasts if AI progress is rapid; the omitted words define the rapid scenario as AI surpassing human performance on many cognitive and physical tasks.

quotes.text: A variance decomposition suggests that expert disagreement about these effects is driven primarily by different beliefs about the economic effects of highly capable AI systems rather than by disagreement about the pace of AI progress.
quotes.speaker: ezra-karger
quotes.context: Abstract: "these effects" are the economic shifts forecast under the rapid scenario. The authors split forecast disagreement into beliefs about AI's pace and beliefs about its economic effects.

quotes.text: Economists strongly favor targeted policy interventions such as AI-focused worker retraining (71.8% support) over broad structural interventions like job guarantees (13.7%) or universal basic income (37.4%), whereas the general public supports both targeted and broad interventions.
quotes.speaker: ezra-karger
quotes.context: Key findings, section 1.3: economists' support for three policy options, set against the general public's.

quotes.text: We also note that worlds with rapid AI progress likely differ from worlds with slow progress in ways that extend beyond AI capabilities themselves, so this gap should be understood as the estimated effect of moving between scenarios that are focused on AI rather than a cleanly identified causal effect of AI capabilities alone.
quotes.speaker: ezra-karger
quotes.context: Footnote to the labor-market results: the around-10-million-jobs figure compares forecasts under the rapid and slow scenarios, and this is what it does not show.

notes: Read the main text in full (introduction to discussion); the appendices (about 8,000 lines of tables, question wording and example rationales) were skimmed, not read in full. Fifteen authors; the quotations are the paper's collective words, attributed to the first-listed author (Ezra Karger, a joint first author with Otto Kuusela), as the Base does for multi-author papers. Check before relying on the 10 million jobs: the abstract and body say roughly half of the participation decline is attributable to AI, but the footnote's own arithmetic gives about 60% (4.2 of 7 percentage points, about 11 million jobs) and rounds it to 10 million; the abstract starts from 62% (February 2026) while the body also cites 62.6% (January 2025). The abstract says the median respondent in every group expects 2.5% GDP growth; the body gives medians of 2.4% to 2.5% for 2030 and up to 3.0% (AI experts) for 2050, which is what the evidence above states. The abstract's rapid-scenario GDP growth of "around 4%" blends groups (economists 3.5%, superforecasters 4.0%, public 4.5%, AI experts 5.3% for 2045-49). The research pass's description also calls this NBER Working Paper 35046; the PDF does not say so. Open Philanthropy is named as funder on the first page. importance 3 is our suggestion: the broadest source in this pass on what informed groups expect and where they disagree.

evidence.design: A survey of forecasts, run online from October 2025 to February 2026 and taking about 8 hours on average: 69 economists, 27 AI industry professionals and 25 AI policy professionals (grouped as 52 AI experts), 38 superforecasters and 401 members of the general public. They forecast US GDP growth, productivity, labor force participation, unemployment, wealth inequality and other outcomes for 2030 and 2050, both overall and conditional on slow, moderate and rapid AI-progress scenarios for 2030, gave their probability of each scenario, and rated six policy proposals. Only the economists' answers are reweighted, for non-response.
evidence.finding: Every group expects substantial AI progress by 2030 (economists give 61.4% on average to the moderate or rapid scenario), yet unconditional forecasts stay near recent trends: median GDP growth of 2.4% to 2.5% to 2030 in every group, and, for economists, labor force participation falling from 62.6% (January 2025) to 61.0% in 2030 and 58.3% in 2050. If AI progress is rapid, economists forecast GDP growth of 3.5% in 2045-49 (superforecasters 4.0%, public 4.5%, AI experts 5.3%) and, for 2050, participation of 55.0%, a labor share of income of 45.0% (55.48% in 2025) and 80.0% of wealth held by the top 10% of households (71.2% in 2023), with a much wider range of outcomes; the authors attribute roughly half of the participation decline, around 10 million jobs, to AI. A variance decomposition finds expert disagreement driven mainly by differing beliefs about the economic effects of highly capable AI, not about the pace of progress. Economists support retraining (71.8%) and modernized unemployment insurance (62.3%) more than basic income (37.4%) or a job guarantee (13.7%); the public supports a job guarantee (57.1%) and favors basic income more than it opposes it (47.9% to 30.3%).
evidence.limits: Forecasts, not measurements: nothing here records what AI has done to jobs so far. The scenarios describe AI capabilities in 2030, not adoption. The authors note that two people choosing "rapid" may have pictured different capabilities, that forecasters may have over-anchored to the historical data shown in the survey, and that the scenarios may miss the most extreme beliefs about capabilities. The 10-million-jobs figure compares the rapid and slow scenarios and, the authors say, is not a cleanly identified causal effect of AI. Only economists were reweighted for non-response; the other groups are small (52 AI experts, 38 superforecasters) and describe the recruited samples, not wider populations. Of 4,866 experts contacted, 147 completed the survey before filtering, and the economist sample skews younger, less experienced, more male and more European than the sampling frame. The public sample came from an online platform. Funded by Open Philanthropy (now Coefficient Giving). A working paper, not edited by the Chicago Fed; its views do not necessarily reflect those of the Chicago Fed or the Federal Reserve System.
evidence.replication: The paper reports no independent replication. It compares with an abridged version of the survey run in a separate panel (LEAP, February 2026): experts there gave the rapid scenario a higher probability, while forecasts conditional on each scenario differed less.

title: Still Waters, Rapid Currents: Early Labor Market Transformation under Generative AI
summary: Humlum and Vestergaard link Statistics Denmark surveys of chatbot use in 11 exposed occupations to administrative earnings and hours records through December 2024. They report that most employers have adopted chatbot initiatives and workers take on new tasks, yet find precise null effects on earnings and hours, ruling out changes above 2%, with occupation switching the one measurable shift.

change.note: Links worker surveys to Danish administrative records: precise null effects on earnings and hours two years after ChatGPT, alongside new tasks and job switching.

lenses.public: Danish workers who use chatbots, even daily, show no clear gap in pay or hours growth from non-users so far; some report new tasks, and some switch occupations.
lenses.policy: The authors say tracking this needs linked data on how work is reorganized inside firms as well as on pay and hours; conventional statistics do not capture the reorganization.
lenses.research: Splitting early-career employment trends by firm adoption, the authors find the declines are not driven by adopters; firms acting in anticipation would bias estimates toward zero.
lenses.ideas: More than a third of the new AI-related tasks workers report involve reviewing AI output or compliance, which raises who is responsible for what the tools produce.

people.title: University of Chicago Booth School of Business and NBER

quotes.text: What does not move is the surface—recorded hours and earnings. Using difference-in-differences, we estimate precise null effects at both the worker and workplace levels, ruling out effects larger than 2% two years after ChatGPT’s launch.
quotes.speaker: anders-humlum
quotes.context: From the conclusion: the main result on earnings and recorded hours, for chatbot users and for workplaces that encourage chatbot use.

quotes.text: While we replicate the pattern of declining early-career employment in exposed occupations in Denmark, our difference-in-differences analysis reveals that the declines are not driven by firms adopting AI chatbots.
quotes.speaker: anders-humlum
quotes.context: From the introduction: the authors split early-career employment declines in Denmark by whether firms adopted chatbots, after a US study documented such declines.

quotes.text: Occupational mobility is the one margin where these rapid currents break through to administrative labor market outcomes: workers who use AI chatbots are more likely to have transitioned into new occupations, particularly into roles where workers have greater discretion over their toolsets.
quotes.speaker: anders-humlum
quotes.context: From the conclusion: the one administrative outcome that moved with adoption, measured by hours in workers' most recent occupation by December 2024.

quotes.text: If so, the absence of measurable labor market effects is not evidence that nothing is happening—but rather that transformation is occurring on margins that conventional economic statistics do not capture.
quotes.speaker: anders-humlum
quotes.context: The authors' conjecture in the conclusion about why stable earnings and hours can coexist with new tasks and occupation switching.

quotes.text: For instance, adopting firms might expand by poaching workers from non-adopting competitors, biasing our workplace employment estimates upward. Alternatively, if firms adjust labor demand in anticipation of AI chatbots—rather than based on their actual adoption—the estimates would be biased toward zero.
quotes.speaker: anders-humlum
quotes.context: The authors name two ways spillovers could bias their workplace estimates, then argue with several checks that spillovers to non-adopters are limited.

notes: Text saved by the research pass: the NBER page gives only the abstract, so the full March 2026 revision text was used. Main text read in full; the online appendix was skimmed. Previously circulated as "Large Language Models, Small Labor Market Effects". Quotations are attributed to the first author on behalf of both. The paper itself says working papers are not peer-reviewed. Its acknowledgements credit Claude Code (Opus 4.6) with research assistance, and a footnote cites a forecast by Anthropic's CEO as one pole of the debate; the entry is not about Anthropic or Claude, so conflict is left false for the editor to decide. Found no earlier Base entry that this clearly bears on.

evidence.design: Statistics Denmark surveys in November-December 2023 and 2024 of workers in 11 AI-exposed occupations (accountants, customer support, financial advisors, HR, IT support, journalists, legal, marketing, office clerks, software developers, teachers); the late-2024 round has 25,000 workers in 7,000 workplaces. Responses are linked to administrative monthly earnings, hours and occupation records through December 2024. Difference-in-differences indexed to ChatGPT's launch in November 2022 compare adopters with non-adopters, and workplaces that encourage chatbot use with those that do not.
evidence.finding: About 43% of employers encourage chatbot use, 21% allow it and 6% prohibit it; even where employers have no initiative, about 41% of workers have used chatbots at work. Earnings, hours and wages: estimates center on zero, with confidence intervals ruling out average effects larger than 2% (3% in the dynamic estimates); the nulls also hold among daily users, and no occupation shows a significant effect. Workplaces encouraging chatbots show no differential change in total hours (effects above 2% ruled out), job churn, or the early-career employment share (effects above a third of a percentage point ruled out). By December 2024 adopters' hours in their most recent occupation were about 4% of a full-time equivalent higher than non-adopters', consistent with more occupation switching, and switchers' earnings grew 12 percentage points faster than other workers'. 97.7% of adopters and 99.5% of non-adopters say chatbots have had no impact on their earnings.
evidence.limits: The design identifies differences between adopters and non-adopters only; any level effect on non-adopters is unidentified, though the authors argue with several checks that it is small. Firms adjusting in anticipation of AI would bias estimates toward zero. The survey records no exact adoption date, employer initiatives are as workers perceive them, outcomes end in December 2024, only 11 highly exposed occupations in Denmark are covered, and occupation-level estimates are wide. The authors conjecture, rather than show, that stable pay and hours coexist with task reorganization that statistics do not record.

title: Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier: Field Experimental Evidence of the Effects of Artificial Intelligence on Knowledge Worker Productivity and Quality

also.title: Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier (HBS Working Paper 24-013, September 2023)

summary: In its abstract, Dell'Acqua and colleagues describe a preregistered experiment with Boston Consulting Group in which 758 knowledge workers were randomly given no AI, GPT-4, or GPT-4 plus prompting guidance. On 18 tasks inside the AI's capabilities, AI users did more, faster and better; on one task outside them, they were 19% less likely to be correct.

change.note: Experiment reports AI helped on tasks inside its capabilities and hurt on one outside them, even within the same workflow: an uneven jagged frontier.

lenses.public: On 18 knowledge tasks AI users did better and faster, but on one complex managerial task they were more often wrong, so knowing when to trust AI may matter.
lenses.policy: A single tool gave mixed results inside one workflow, which bears on training and oversight for workers who use AI; the evidence is from one collaboration and GPT-4 tools.
lenses.research: The jagged-frontier framing and preregistered randomized design offer a template for testing where AI helps or hurts knowledge work; the abstract does not separate the three study arms.

people.title: Digital Data Design Institute, Harvard Business School
Digital Data Design Institute, Harvard Business School
The Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania
Digital Data Design Institute, Harvard Business School; Warwick Business School
Sloan School of Management, Massachusetts Institute of Technology
Digital Data Design Institute, Harvard Business School

quotes.text: For each one of a set of 18 realistic knowledge tasks within the frontier of AI capabilities ranging from creative to analytical tasks, subjects using AI outperformed those not using AI, completing 12.2% more tasks and completing them 25.1% more quickly on average while also delivering solutions of significantly improved quality.
quotes.speaker: fabrizio-dellacqua
quotes.context: The authors' abstract: results on the tasks designed to lie inside the AI's capabilities.

quotes.text: However, for a complex managerial task selected to be outside the frontier, subjects using AI were 19% less likely to produce correct solutions compared with those without AI, pointing to potential limitations of AI supporting knowledge workers.
quotes.speaker: fabrizio-dellacqua
quotes.context: The authors' abstract: the result on the single task chosen to lie outside the AI's capabilities.

quotes.text: We introduce and study the concept of a “jagged technology frontier” to describe the uneven impact of artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities, where AI assistance improves performance for some tasks but worsens it for others, even within the same knowledge workflow and with a seemingly similar level of difficulty.
quotes.speaker: fabrizio-dellacqua
quotes.context: The opening sentence of the authors' abstract, defining the concept the paper is built on.

notes: Abstract only. The article page (INFORMS), SSRN and the Harvard Business School PDF returned 403 or a bot-check response, so no full text was read. The saved text is the publisher's Crossref record (bibliographic data, author affiliations and abstract); the abstract is identical to the one on the Harvard Business School page for the 2023 working paper (HBS Working Paper 24-013, September 2023, 58 pages; https://www.hbs.edu/faculty/Pages/item.aspx?num=64700, which lists the Organization Science version as March-April 2026). The date 2026-03 is Crossref's issue month. The abstract does not say that the 758 participants were BCG consultants (the triage does); check the full text. Three authors are at BCG's Henderson Institute and the study was run in collaboration with BCG; the Crossref record states funding from the Harvard Business School Digital Data Design Institute and its Division of Research and Faculty Development. All quotations are from the abstract.

evidence.design: A preregistered randomized experiment with 758 knowledge workers, run in collaboration with Boston Consulting Group on management-consulting tasks the authors developed. After a performance baseline on similar tasks, participants were randomly assigned to no AI access, GPT-4 access, or GPT-4 access with a prompt-engineering overview. They did 18 realistic tasks, from creative to analytical, inside the AI's capability frontier, and one complex managerial task chosen to lie outside it. Based on the abstract only; the full text was not readable.
evidence.finding: On the 18 tasks inside the frontier, participants using AI completed 12.2% more tasks and finished 25.1% more quickly on average, with significantly higher-quality solutions. On the one task chosen to lie outside the frontier, participants using AI were 19% less likely to produce correct solutions than those without AI.
evidence.limits: Abstract only, so the paper's own limitations, sample details and results by study arm are not reflected. From the design as described: the outside-the-frontier result rests on a single task chosen by the researchers; the tasks were built by the authors with one firm; and the AI was GPT-4. The abstract gives no effect sizes for the arm with prompting guidance and no intervals.

title: Bridging Skill Gaps for the Future: New Jobs Creation in the AI Age
summary: An IMF Staff Discussion Note analyses online job postings in six countries. It finds roughly 1 in 10 postings in advanced economies asks for a skill new to the labor market, and such skills go with higher pay; greater demand for new AI skills has not raised overall US employment and goes with lower employment in some exposed occupations.

change.note: New cross-country vacancy evidence: AI-skill demand pays more but has not raised overall US employment, and goes with lower employment in exposed jobs.

lenses.public: Jobs asking for AI skills pay more, but US regions with more AI-skill demand had lower employment in jobs highly exposed to AI, which the note says challenges young workers.
lenses.policy: The note urges worker mobility, lifelong learning, limits on non-compete agreements and stronger social protection, with priorities depending on a country's Skill Imbalance Index.
lenses.research: Shift-share and event-study designs on US commuting zones link posting-based AI-skill demand to American Community Survey employment; online postings overrepresent higher-skill work.
lenses.ideas: The note closes by saying work provides not only income but also dignity and purpose, and that the role of AI in society needs examining, not only skills policy.

quotes.text: In data provided by Lightcast, roughly 1 in 10 job postings requires at least one new skill in advanced economies, and the incidence is about half of that for emerging market economies.
quotes.speaker: florence-jaumotte
quotes.context: The Executive Summary: how common new skills are in online job postings, from the Lightcast data the note rests on.

quotes.text: Although vacancies demanding new AI-related skills post higher wages, they have so far not boosted overall employment in US local labor markets.
quotes.speaker: florence-jaumotte
quotes.context: The Executive Summary: what demand for new AI skills has and has not done for overall US employment.

quotes.text: Further, the empirical analysis shows that—for occupations that are highly exposed to AI, but with limited scope for complementarity—employment levels are 3.6 percent lower in regions with greater demand for AI-related skills than in other regions five years after the appearance of these skills.
quotes.speaker: florence-jaumotte
quotes.context: The Executive Summary: the note's employment result for occupations highly exposed to AI with little room for complementarity.

quotes.text: These skills boost average wages and employment but deepen polarization, mostly benefitting high- and—through higher consumption of services—low-skilled workers, and potentially contributing to the shrinking of the middle class.
quotes.speaker: florence-jaumotte
quotes.context: The abstract: what new skills overall do to wages, employment and who benefits.

quotes.text: Because Lightcast relies on online job postings, the data provide a detailed picture of skill demand in the formal economy but naturally overrepresent professional, technical, and higher-skill occupations.
quotes.speaker: florence-jaumotte
quotes.context: The Introduction's limitations paragraph: what the vacancy data cover.

notes: Text: the IMF eLibrary HTML edition of Staff Discussion Note 2026/001 (imf.org and its PDF return 403 to scripted requests; the eLibrary PDF did not download), read in full apart from the annex data tables. Publication date 14 Jan 2026 and DOI 10.5089/9798229028196.006.A001 are from that page; the imf.org address carries 2026/01/09, so the editor may want to check which day the IMF itself gives. The page shows an affiliation only for the first author; all eight are given the IMF because this is an IMF staff note. The page text carries no statement that the note reflects the authors' views and not IMF policy; the research pass reported one in the PDF, which was not read. Quotations use the first author's id. The 6.3% is per percentage point of AI-skill demand; the 3.6% is the predicted effect for the observed rise (0.57 points). The 40%, 60% and 28% exposure shares the note repeats are the IMF's 2024 estimates, not new here. The note cites the NBER ChatGPT paper in this pass (Chatterji and others, 2025) for the speed of AI adoption and the ILO's 2023 exposure study; the editor may want to relate them.

evidence.design: Staff analysis of online job postings from Lightcast in six countries (United States, United Kingdom, Germany, Brazil, Denmark, South Africa) to find skills barely present in 2010-11, matched to posted wages; local labor market regressions on US commuting zones (American Community Survey, 2013-23) and 96 German regions (administrative records, 2019-23) with shift-share instruments for new skills; an event study of AI-skill entry on US employment; firm records (Compustat) and nearly 18 million US worker profiles; and skill demand and supply measures for 36 countries.
evidence.finding: About 1 in 10 postings in advanced economies lists a new skill, about half that in emerging economies; AI skills were in under 1% of US postings before 2015 and almost 5% by 2025. A new skill goes with 3 to 3.4% higher wage offers in the US and UK. In US local labor markets a 1 point rise in postings with new skills goes with 2.3% higher wages and 1.3% higher employment, gains for high- and low-skilled but not middle-skilled workers. For AI skills alone there is no gain in overall employment: where AI-skill demand is 1 point higher, employment in occupations highly exposed to AI with limited complementarity (about 30% of employment, per the IMF's 2024 work) is 6.3% lower after five years, about 3.6% for the observed rise. AI-skill wage premiums are about 7.5 to 8% in the UK and, in the US, above 8% for developer skills but about 2% for user skills.
evidence.limits: Measures vacancies and regional employment levels, not layoffs; the note describes the AI result as employment linked to AI-skill demand, and calls its evidence on local adjustment early. Online postings overrepresent formal, urban and higher-skill work, more so in emerging markets, coverage varies by country, and firms that fill jobs internally may be understated. The AI employment result is for US commuting zones; the German analysis covers new skills in general and finds no significant employment effect, which the note says may reflect the short time span and labor market rigidities. The skill indices compare countries with the US as benchmark and cannot quantify mismatches in headcount.

title: Tracking AI’s Contribution to GDP Growth
outlet: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis
summary: Two St. Louis Fed researchers add up the growth contributions of information-processing equipment, software, R&D and data-center investment as AI-related spending. They report these supplied 39% of real GDP growth in the first three quarters of 2025 (36% without data centers) against 28% in 2000, which has no data-center figure, and fell back in the third quarter.

change.note: AI-related investment supplied 39% of US real GDP growth in the first three quarters of 2025 (36% without data centers) against 28% in 2000.

lenses.public: Business spending on AI-related equipment, software, research and data centers supplied 39% of US growth in the first three quarters of 2025. It measures spending, not what AI tools produce.
lenses.policy: Uses federal statistics to show how much recent US growth rests on AI-related investment; the authors expect these categories to stay significant into 2026 and beyond.
lenses.research: Growth accounting with broad categories as stand-ins for AI spending (not all R&D is AI-related), an imputed September data-center figure, and a 2000 comparison without data centers.

people.title: Economist, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis
Research associate, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis

quotes.text: Together, the AI categories contributed 0.97 percentage points to real GDP growth in the first three quarters of 2025 (0.90 percentage points, excluding data centers, for which data were not available in 2000), higher than the 0.81 percentage points in 2000.
quotes.speaker: hannah-rubinton
