quotes.context: The authors' headline comparison with the dot-com year 2000; the 2000 figure has no data-center component.

quotes.text: Through the third quarter of 2025, these categories made up 39% (36% excluding data centers) of total GDP growth versus 28% in 2000.
quotes.speaker: hannah-rubinton
quotes.context: The same comparison as a share of total real GDP growth.

quotes.text: Together the four categories contributed 1.3 percentage points to real GDP growth in the first quarter of 2025 and 1.16 percentage points to real GDP growth in the second quarter, but the combined contribution leveled off to 0.48 percentage points in the third quarter.
quotes.speaker: hannah-rubinton
quotes.context: The quarter-by-quarter pattern of the four categories' combined contribution.

quotes.text: Our analysis suggests that the recent investments in AI-related categories have contributed significantly to the real GDP growth in 2025. It has surpassed the contribution of IT components to the real GDP growth made during the dot-com boom, both in levels and as a share of GDP.
quotes.speaker: hannah-rubinton
quotes.context: The authors' conclusion in the closing section.

notes: The St. Louis Fed site would not serve a scripted fetch (an HTTP/2 stream error, then a timeout) and the research pass's text file for it was empty, so the text is the Internet Archive's copy of the page, captured 12 October 2026 (Wayback), which shows the date January 12, 2026 and both authors. Compare it with the live page if the wording matters. The quarterly figures re-add to the post's totals (1.30, 1.16 and 0.48 points; 0.97 over the nine months). The 39% vs 28% comparison is not like for like, since 2000 has no data-center figure; the post gives the like-for-like 36% and 0.90 points beside it. The saved text includes the page's menus and the formula spread over lines. The post is about the investment boom's contribution to GDP, not about employment.

evidence.design: Growth accounting. For information-processing equipment, software and R&D (Bureau of Economic Analysis) and data-center construction (Census Bureau, from 2014), the authors compute each category's contribution to real GDP growth in annualized percentage points, using a Fisher-Tornqvist formula, for the first three quarters of 2025, and compare the average with the four quarters of 2000, the height of the dot-com boom.
evidence.finding: The four categories together contributed 1.3, 1.16 and 0.48 percentage points to real GDP growth in the first, second and third quarters of 2025: 0.97 points, or 39% of growth (36% without data centers), over the three quarters, against 0.81 points, 28%, in 2000. The authors say the third-quarter fall reflects slower investment growth, not lower investment levels, which stayed elevated.
evidence.limits: The categories are broad stand-ins for AI spending; the authors note not all R&D is AI-related. The September 2025 data-center figure was imputed from July and August. The 2000 comparison has no data-center component, so the like-for-like figures are 0.90 vs 0.81 points and 36% vs 28%. It measures investment's contribution to growth, not AI's effect on productivity, jobs or incomes. A blog post that says its views are not necessarily those of the St. Louis Fed or the Federal Reserve System.

title: How People Use ChatGPT
summary: An NBER working paper by mostly OpenAI-affiliated authors uses automated classifiers, with no person reading the text, on a random sample of consumer ChatGPT messages. The authors report that messages unrelated to work grew from 53% to 73% of daily volume between June 2024 and June 2025, and that writing is the most common work use.

change.note: Authors say it is the first economics paper using ChatGPT's internal message data; finds most consumer use is not work-related.

lenses.public: Most consumer ChatGPT use is advice, information and writing help, and over 70% of messages are not about work, so user counts alone say little about jobs.
lenses.policy: Adoption statistics should not be read as labor-market exposure: this data, which excludes business and enterprise plans, shows what people ask, not which tasks replace paid work.
lenses.research: A privacy-preserving method for studying chatbot use at scale, validated on a public chat dataset; the work/non-work label is automated, and no pay or output outcomes are measured.
lenses.ideas: The authors note most economic analysis of AI looks at paid work, and argue its effect on activity outside work is of similar scale and possibly larger.

OpenAI and Harvard Society of Fellows

quotes.text: We find steady growth in work-related messages but even faster growth in non-work-related messages, which have grown from 53% to more than 70% of all usage.
quotes.speaker: aaron-chatterji
quotes.context: The abstract: how the share of consumer ChatGPT messages unrelated to work changed; the body dates the 53% to June 2024 and the 73% to June 2025.

quotes.text: Writing is the most common use case at work, accounting for 40% of work-related messages on average in June 2025.
quotes.speaker: aaron-chatterji
quotes.context: The introduction, on what users do with ChatGPT at work, from the classified sample of messages.

quotes.text: Work usage is more common for educated users in highly-paid professional occupations.
quotes.speaker: aaron-chatterji
quotes.context: The abstract: who uses ChatGPT for work, from aggregated employment and education categories matched through a data clean room.

quotes.text: Our sample includes the three consumer plans (Free, Plus, or Pro). OpenAI also offers a variety of other ChatGPT plans (Business fka. Teams, Enterprise, Education), which we do not include in our sample.
quotes.speaker: aaron-chatterji
quotes.context: Footnote 5: the study covers consumer plans only, not the plans that businesses, enterprises and schools use.

quotes.text: Our categories often apply to the user’s intention, rather than the text of the conversation, and as such we never directly observe the ground truth.
quotes.speaker: aaron-chatterji
quotes.context: Section 5: the authors on their message categories, which apply to the user's intention and are best-guess inferences, not directly observed.

notes: Text: the NBER PDF (w34255.pdf), word for word the copy the research pass saved; read in full. The PDF says NBER working papers are not peer reviewed. Status company-report: the data are OpenAI's, six of the seven authors list an OpenAI affiliation, and the NBER page discloses that Chatterji (Duke and OpenAI) and Hitzig (OpenAI) are OpenAI employees. Quotations use the first author's id though the paper has seven authors. The paper is loose with itself in two places: the abstract and introduction put the three top topics at nearly 80% of use, Section 5.2 at about 77% and the conclusion at nearly 78%; the conclusion gives Expressing as 1% of messages where Section 5.3 says 11%. The entry uses the body numbers. User counts are accounts and may exceed people (the paper's footnote 20). Appendix A reproduces the study's classifier prompts; they are part of the paper and were not acted on. The IMF note and the World Bank report in this pass both cite this paper (the IMF for the speed of AI adoption, the World Bank for people using AI for practical advice, information and everyday tasks); the editor may want to relate them.

evidence.design: Language-model classifiers sorted a random sample of about 1.1 million consumer ChatGPT messages (May 2024 to June 2025) by work or non-work, topic, intent and O*NET work activity, with no person reading the messages. Daily message counts cover all consumer users since November 2022, and aggregated job and education categories for about 130,000 users came through a secure data clean room.
evidence.finding: By July 2025 ChatGPT had more than 700 million weekly users sending 18 billion messages a week, about 10% of the world's adults. Non-work messages rose from 53% of daily volume in June 2024 (238 of 451 million messages) to 73% in June 2025 (1,911 of 2,627 million); work messages also grew, from 213 to 716 million. Practical guidance, seeking information and writing make up about 77% of conversations, and writing is about 40% of work messages. The work share is 37% for users without a bachelor's degree against 48% for those with graduate study, and 57% for computer-related occupations against 40% for non-professional ones (unadjusted).
evidence.limits: Written partly by OpenAI employees from OpenAI's own data, so a company report even though NBER circulates it as an unreviewed working paper. Covers consumer plans only: Business, Enterprise and Education plans, logged-out users, under-18s and users who opted out of training are excluded. Whether a message is work-related is a language model's judgment from the message and its context, checked against 149 conversations from a public dataset (agreement with the human majority 0.83 on Cohen's kappa; humans among themselves 0.66). The education and occupation results cover a subset of users (about 130,000, and about 40,000 in the regressions) that may not be representative. The paper measures no productivity, pay, hours or job outcomes; its claim that ChatGPT raises worker output by supporting decisions is the authors' argument.

title: Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity
summary: METR researchers report a randomized trial in which 16 experienced open-source developers completed 246 real tasks in mature repositories, each task randomly allowing or barring early-2025 AI tools. Tasks took 19% longer with AI allowed, although developers had expected a 24% saving. The authors caution against generalizing beyond this setting.

change.note: Randomized trial finds experienced developers took 19% longer with early-2025 AI tools while believing they were faster; applies to one narrow setting.

lenses.public: Skilled workers can feel faster with AI while measuring slower, so impressions can mislead, though this trial covers one kind of expert work, not jobs in general.
lenses.policy: The authors say field experiments with robust measures matter more than relying only on expert forecasts or user surveys; experts predicted time savings near 40%.
lenses.research: Tasks were defined before random assignment, which fixes the outcome measure in advance; but the estimate rests on 16 developers and February-June 2025 tools.

quotes.text: Surprisingly, we find that allowing AI actually increases completion time by 19%—AI tooling slowed developers down.
quotes.speaker: joel-becker
quotes.context: The authors' abstract: the main result of the trial.

quotes.text: Before starting tasks, developers forecast that allowing AI will reduce completion time by 24%. After completing the study, developers estimate that allowing AI reduced completion time by 20%.
quotes.speaker: joel-becker
quotes.context: The authors' abstract: what the developers themselves expected before and believed after.

quotes.text: This slowdown also contradicts predictions from experts in economics (39% shorter) and ML (38% shorter).
quotes.speaker: joel-becker
quotes.context: The authors' abstract: how the result compares with forecasts from economics and machine-learning experts.

quotes.text: Although the influence of experimental artifacts cannot be entirely ruled out, the robustness of the slowdown effect across our analyses suggests it is unlikely to primarily be a function of our experimental design.
quotes.speaker: joel-becker
quotes.context: The authors' abstract: their view of whether the study design explains the slowdown.

quotes.text: That said, many of the factors we find evidence for contributing to slowdown are specific to the setting we study—these results do not imply that current AI systems are not useful in many realistic, economically relevant settings.
quotes.speaker: joel-becker
quotes.context: Introduction: the authors limit what the result shows about AI's usefulness beyond this setting.

notes: Version read: arXiv v2, 25 Jul 2025 (v1 was submitted 12 Jul 2025, which is the triage date). The arXiv abstract page says 20 properties were examined; the v2 paper says 21 (5 contribute, 10 unclear, 6 against), and this entry follows the paper. The saved text does not mention METR's February 2026 follow-up. Read separately, not part of the saved text: METR's post of 24 Feb 2026 (https://metr.org/blog/2026-02-24-uplift-update/) says a newer experiment begun in August 2025 gives an unreliable signal of the current effect, mainly because more developers declined to take part if it meant working without AI; it reports raw estimates that show a speedup with wide intervals, says developers are likely more sped up in early 2026 than in early 2025, and says METR is changing its study design. An editor may want that post as its own entry. The tools used in the trial included Anthropic's Claude 3.5 and 3.7 Sonnet, but the paper is not about Anthropic.

evidence.design: A randomized controlled trial. Sixteen experienced open-source developers (about five years on their own repository on average; repositories averaging 23,000 stars and 1.1 million lines of code) completed 246 real tasks of about two hours each, with AI tools of the February-June 2025 frontier. Each task was randomly assigned to allow or disallow AI tools; developers chose their tools (mostly Cursor Pro with Claude 3.5 or 3.7 Sonnet) and were paid $150 an hour. Time to finish was self-reported; screen recordings were used to check compliance and, for a subset, the reported times.
evidence.finding: Allowing AI increased completion time by 19%. Developers had forecast a 24% reduction beforehand and estimated a 20% reduction afterwards; economics experts predicted 39% shorter and machine-learning experts 38% shorter. In per-developer estimates, 75% of developers were slowed down. On a subset of recorded tasks, developers with AI allowed spent less time actively coding and searching for information and more time prompting, waiting for and reviewing AI output. The authors name five factors they judge to contribute, including over-optimism about AI, high familiarity with the repositories, and large, complex codebases, and call this analysis speculative.
evidence.limits: Sixteen developers working on mature repositories they knew well, with February-June 2025 tools; developers knew which condition applied. The authors say the slowdown does not imply AI fails to help in other settings (small new projects or unfamiliar codebases may see speedups), that better or later systems could speed up developers even here, and that experimental artifacts cannot be entirely ruled out, including the chance that developers who rely heavily on AI were less likely to take part. They call the factor analysis suggestive only, because the data are not powered for multiple comparisons, and they study software development only.

title: Generative AI and Jobs: A Refined Global Index of Occupational Exposure

also.title: ILO Working Paper 140: publication page

summary: An ILO working paper, written with Poland's research institute NASK, updates the ILO's 2023 index of how far generative AI could perform each occupation's tasks. Scoring tasks by survey, expert review and AI models, the authors find 24% of global employment has some exposure, 3.3% the highest, and judge transformation of jobs likelier than replacement.

change.note: Revises the ILO's 2023 estimate: 24% of jobs have some GenAI exposure, 3.3% the highest; the authors stress this is exposure, not impact.

lenses.public: About one in four workers is in an occupation where AI could do some tasks, clerical work most; the authors think changed jobs likelier than lost ones.
lenses.policy: The figures are an upper bound on possible effects, not job-loss forecasts; the authors urge social dialogue and targeted policy, and find women and richer countries more exposed.
lenses.research: Scores blend a survey of 1,640 Polish workers, expert review and AI models; all tasks are weighted equally, and task-level scores are public for reuse.
lenses.ideas: If a job is a bundle of tasks, automating some can reshape work rather than end it, though the tasks left over may make a job unsustainable or undesirable.

quotes.text: Globally, one in four workers are in an occupation with some GenAI exposure. 3.3% of global employment falls into the highest exposure category, albeit with significant differences between female (4.7%) and male employment (2.4%).
quotes.speaker: pawel-gmyrek
quotes.context: The abstract's headline result: the share of global employment in occupations with some generative AI exposure, and in the highest category.

quotes.text: Indeed, the results indicate that few jobs consist of tasks that are fully automatable with current GenAI technology; nearly all occupations have some tasks that require human input.
quotes.speaker: pawel-gmyrek
quotes.context: In the section on revised global employment estimates, on what the task scores show about whole jobs.

quotes.text: Clerical occupations continue to have the highest exposure levels. Additionally, some strongly digitized occupations have increased exposure, highlighting the expanding abilities of GenAI regarding specialized tasks in professional and technical roles.
quotes.speaker: pawel-gmyrek
quotes.context: The abstract: which occupations score highest, and which digitized professional jobs rose since the ILO's 2023 study.

quotes.text: It is important to stress that these new estimates reflect “exposure” to GenAI and not the actual impact on employment. As in 2023, the 2025 estimates represent the upper threshold of the percentage of employment that could be affected if GenAI technology were fully implemented.
quotes.speaker: pawel-gmyrek
quotes.context: From the section on revised global employment estimates: what the figures do and do not measure.

quotes.text: Finally, the estimates do not account for new jobs that may be created, nor the technological advances that could potentially automate more tasks in the future. In that sense, our estimates present a static snapshot of the exposure of existing occupations to GenAI at the start of 2025.
quotes.speaker: pawel-gmyrek
quotes.context: Closing paragraph of the global employment estimates: the time frame and what the estimates leave out.

notes: Text: the ILO's HTML edition of Working Paper 140 (Read online), read in full apart from the annex tables. The paper itself gives only the year (copyright 2025); the day, 20 May 2025, comes from the ILO publication page, which also lists Balint Nafradi among the authors; the paper's byline and author notes name seven people, and Nafradi is included here on the publication page's word, without a title. Quotations use the first author's id. Scores partly come from AI models (the authors say the writing and calculations are their own). The World Bank report in this pass builds its jobs shares on this ILO-NASK index, and the IMF note in this pass cites the ILO's 2023 study; the editor may want to relate them.

evidence.design: A task-level exposure index. A web survey of employed people in Poland on an online research platform (1,535 retained of 1,640; 52,558 task ratings) scored a sample of 2,861 of the 29,753 tasks in the Polish occupational classification; experts reviewed 608 tasks; two AI models (GPT-4o and Gemini Flash 1.5) reconciled survey and expert scores; an AI assistant then predicted scores for all tasks in the international ISCO-08 classification. Occupations are sorted into four exposure gradients by the mean and spread of their task scores, and the ILO global employment model turns that into shares of employment by sex, region and income group.
evidence.finding: 24% of global employment is in an occupation with some generative AI exposure (gradients 1 to 4): 3.3% in the highest gradient (4.7% of female and 2.4% of male employment) and 20.5% in the lower three. Exposure is 34% of employment in high-income countries and 11% in low-income ones; in high-income countries 9.6% of female and 3.5% of male employment is in the highest gradient. Clerical jobs stay the most exposed, with data entry clerks, typists and bookkeeping clerks among 13 occupations in the top gradient. The 2023 estimate was 2.3% in its automation category and 29.2% across augmentation and an unknown middle category.
evidence.limits: Exposure is a score for existing tasks, not employment impact: the authors call the estimates an upper threshold, say they leave out new jobs and later advances, and describe them as a static snapshot at the start of 2025. Scores rest on a Polish survey (76% of respondents never or rarely used generative AI), expert judgment and AI-model arbitration, weight every task equally, and treat Poland as an upper-threshold setting. Exposure does not say whether workers will be replaced or retrained; the authors think transformation likelier but warn that partial automation could still cut demand for some jobs.

title: Generative AI at Work

also.title: Generative AI at Work (journal version, volume 140, issue 2, 2025)

summary: Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond (arXiv version of their 2025 Quarterly Journal of Economics paper) study a GPT-based chat assistant introduced in stages to 5,172 customer-support agents at one company. They report 15% more issues resolved per hour on average, with the largest gains for less experienced agents, and say the data cannot show wage or employment effects.

change.note: Workplace evidence that AI assistance raised output most for newer, lower-skilled workers in one firm; wage and employment effects not measured.

lenses.public: In one company's support center, an AI assistant helped newer and lower-skilled workers most and top performers little, though the study cannot say whether pay, hours or jobs changed.
lenses.policy: Gains can narrow gaps between workers inside one firm, but the study measures no wage, hiring or layoff effects, so it cannot alone guide training or labor-market policy.
lenses.research: A staggered rollout across 5,172 agents shows larger gains for novices, but covers one tool, one firm and one occupation, with no pay data.
lenses.ideas: The authors ask whether workers whose practices train an AI system should be paid for that data, since the tool may dull top performers' incentive to contribute new solutions.

quotes.text: Access to AI assistance increases worker productivity, as measured by issues resolved per hour, by 15% on average, with substantial heterogeneity across workers.
quotes.speaker: erik-brynjolfsson
quotes.context: The authors' abstract: the average effect of the AI assistant at the firm studied.

quotes.text: Less experienced and lower-skilled workers improve both the speed and quality of their output while the most experienced and highest-skilled workers see small gains in speed and small declines in quality.
quotes.speaker: erik-brynjolfsson
quotes.context: The authors' abstract: how the effect differs by agent experience and skill.

quotes.text: We emphasize, however, that these findings capture medium run impacts within a single firm: our paper is not designed to shed light on the aggregate employment or wage effects of generative AI tools.
quotes.speaker: erik-brynjolfsson
quotes.context: The authors on what the study cannot show, in the introduction.

quotes.text: If customer demand for assistance is inelastic, then the productivity gains we document will likely translate into less demand for human labor. A back-of-the-envelope calculation suggests the firm could field the same number of customer support issues with 12% fewer worker-hours.
quotes.speaker: erik-brynjolfsson
quotes.context: Conclusion: the authors' rough labor calculation, which applies if customer demand is inelastic; they add that better service could instead raise demand for support and for labor.

quotes.text: First, we note again that our findings apply for a particular AI tool, used in a single firm, within a single occupation, and should not be generalized across all occupations and AI systems.
quotes.speaker: erik-brynjolfsson
quotes.context: Conclusion: the first of the authors' stated caveats.

notes: Version read: arXiv v2, stamped 6 Nov 2024 (the title page in the PDF says November 7, 2024). The HTML rendering shows August 24, 2026 under the authors' names, which is a build date, not the paper's. The paper appeared in The Quarterly Journal of Economics 140(2), pages 889-942 (doi 10.1093/qje/qjae044); Crossref gives 4 Feb 2025 as the online date (the triage date) and 8 Apr 2025 for print. The journal page returned 403, so the journal text was not read. The journal abstract differs from the v2 abstract in places (it says gains are largest for moderately rare problems where the system still has adequate training data, where v2 says relatively rare problems, and it adds that effects vary significantly across agents), while the main figures match (5,172 agents, 15%); check the journal text before relying on details beyond those. The roughly 30% gain for less experienced and lower-skilled agents is in the introduction, not the abstract; the lowest skill quintile is 36%. The paper gives the adherence rate as 35% in one place and 38% in another, so it is not used here. The saved text is the arXiv HTML rendering, with footnote numbers inside some sentences; the quotations avoid them.

evidence.design: A staggered, agent-by-agent rollout of a GPT-based chat assistant (suggested replies and links to documentation, which agents could ignore) at a Fortune 500 business-software firm and its subcontractors, mostly in the fall of 2020 and winter of 2021. Productivity before and after access is compared across 5,172 customer-support agents and about 3 million chats (difference-in-differences), with a small randomized pilot of about 50 workers as a check.
evidence.finding: Access raised issues resolved per hour by 15% on average (0.30 more chats an hour, 15.2% in the preferred specification). The paper puts the gain at about 30% for less-skilled and less-experienced agents (36% in the lowest skill quintile) and finds minimal impact for the most experienced or skilled agents, whose conversation quality fell slightly. Agents with two months of tenure and AI assistance performed as well as untreated agents with more than six months. Average resolution rates and surveyed customer satisfaction showed no economically significant change. Customer sentiment improved by about half a standard deviation, requests to speak to a manager fell by almost 25%, and attrition among agents with under six months of tenure fell by about 10 percentage points, a result the authors say calls for more caution.
evidence.limits: One AI tool, one firm and one occupation, over the short to medium run; the authors say the findings should not be generalized. The data hold no pay information and cannot show changes in overall labor demand or in the skill mix of new hires. The authors add that if customer demand is inelastic the gains would likely mean less demand for human labor (their rough calculation: the same issues handled with 12% fewer worker-hours), while better service could instead raise demand for support and for labor. Managers chose who was trained first, which the authors address with an instrumental-variable check and the pilot. The text-similarity analysis is described as only suggestive.
evidence.replication: The paper says several lab-like studies (by Noy and Zhang, Choi and Schwarcz, Peng and co-authors, and Dell'Acqua and co-authors) find the same pattern of gains concentrated among lower-skill workers, and calls itself the first study of longer-term effects in a real workplace.
